name: Bhai Taru Singh
summary: A young farmer from near Amritsar who fed hiding Sikhs, refused to give up his uncut hair, and is remembered as a martyr of 1745.
about: Bhai Taru Singh was born around 1720 near Amritsar and farmed a small plot of maize at Poolha, near Kasur. According to Sikh history, he and his sister Tar Kaur fed and helped Sikhs who were hiding from the Mughal rulers of Punjab. He was reported to the governor of Lahore, Zakariya Khan, and arrested. Sikh tradition says he refused to ask for pardon and refused to cut his uncut hair, the kesh Sikhs keep as a gift from Guru Gobind Singh. He was executed in Lahore in 1745 by having his scalp removed. Sikh sources tell that the governor died soon after, as Taru Singh had foretold. Historians note that the details, including the date and the informer's name, differ between accounts. He is remembered in Sikh tradition as a shaheed, a martyr, and Lahore keeps his memory in Shahidganj.
kidSummary: Taru Singh was a farmer who helped hungry Sikhs hiding in the forest. When rulers told him to cut his hair and give up his faith, he said no. Sikhs remember him for being brave and kind and for standing by what he believed.

story.title: A farmer with a kind heart
story.text: Taru Singh grew maize on a small farm near Kasur. He shared his food with Sikhs who were hiding in the forests.

story.title: Helped by his sister
story.text: His sister Tar Kaur helped him cook and carry food. Together they kept travellers and fighters fed.

story.title: Taken to Lahore
story.text: A man told the governor about them, and soldiers took Taru Singh to Lahore. He did not ask to be forgiven.

story.title: Strong because of his hair
story.text: The governor threatened him, but Taru Singh said he would not part with even one hair, the kesh Sikhs keep as a gift of Guru Gobind Singh.

story.title: Remembered in Lahore
story.text: Sikh history says Taru Singh died in 1745. The square where he was scalped is part of Shahidganj, where Sikhs remember many martyrs, and a gurdwara marks the spot.

family.name: His widowed mother (name not given in the sources)

facts.text: His widowed mother and his sister ground grain to earn a living, and the little they made was still sent to the Sikhs hiding in the forests.
Governor Zakariya Khan once asked his men why the Sikhs were not starving, since he had cut off their work, taxes and offerings. An informer then pointed to Taru Singh's village.

In the Damdami Taksal account his jailers offered him a noble Mughal bride, wealth and rank if he would change faith and cut his hair, and warned that otherwise there would be forced cutting, worse torture and finally beheading or the wheel. He refused it all.
The Damdami Taksal account says the governor finally said Taru Singh's hair would stay uncut, since the whole scalp with its hair would be scraped off. Taru Singh calmly told him to do as he liked.
The historian Ratan Singh Bhangu wrote that Taru Singh cursed Zakariya Khan, saying he would be brought down by shoes.

Sikh sources say the governor soon fell ill with severe pain and could not pass urine, and begged the Sikhs for forgiveness. He was told to strike himself with Taru Singh's shoes, and died 22 days later. Wikipedia marks the shoes detail as needing a citation.

A print showing his martyrdom hangs in a Sikh temple scene of the 2007 film The Darjeeling Limited, and a 3D-animated film about his life, directed by Vismaad Singh, came out worldwide on 27 April 2018.

According to the Damdami Taksal account, he carried cakes of wheat and gram flour and a bucket of milk into the forest at night, sat and talked with the hidden Sikhs, and warned them whenever he heard of a new government move against them.
Governor Zakariya Khan offered rewards for betraying Sikhs. One reward was a blanket for anyone who cut off a Sikh's long hair, and a bigger one for delivering a Sikh skull.
Sikh lore says that when a barber tried to cut his hair it became as strong as iron, and the angry governor ordered his scalp removed instead. Wikipedia flags this detail as needing a citation.
The Damdami Taksal account says a shoemaker removed his scalp while he went on reciting Japji, and that afterwards he thanked God that his hair had not been cut.
When the sick governor sent a message asking for forgiveness, Taru Singh answered that he held no hatred and forgave him, though he said everyone must answer for their deeds.
The daily Sikh Ardas recalls those whose scalps were removed for their faith, and SikhNet links that line of the prayer to Bhai Taru Singh.
Wikipedia says that when the governor asked where he found the strength to bear the pain, Taru Singh answered that it came from his uncut hair, blessed by Guru Gobind Singh.
In SikhNet's retelling, when he was told to convert or die, he replied that giving up his faith would not save him from death, because everyone dies.
SikhNet says he greeted the governor with the Khalsa salute, Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh, and that this made the governor furious.
One telling in the Chhota Ghallughara page says he walked out of his village to give himself up to the soldiers, so that his neighbours would not suffer.
The same page says that after the scalping he was left to die and was handed to a Sikh family, who looked after him for his last days.
SikhNet says he took Amrit from Bhai Mani Singh and was deeply moved by Mani Singh's own martyrdom in 1737, linking the two stories.
Two gurdwaras honoured him in Lahore: Shaheedganj Bhai Taru Singh in Naulakha Bazaar and Shaheed Bhai Taru Singh near Hanuman Gali. Only the gateway of the second still stands.

quiz.q: What crop did Bhai Taru Singh grow on his small farm?
quiz.why: He grew maize at Poolha near Kasur.

quiz.q: What would Bhai Taru Singh not let anyone cut?
quiz.why: He kept his kesh, a gift linked to Guru Gobind Singh, and refused to give it up.

quiz.q: What is the name of his sister?
Which film shows a print of his martyrdom in a Sikh temple?
quiz.why: The 2007 film The Darjeeling Limited shows it.

quiz.q: In which city was Bhai Taru Singh scalped?
quiz.why: He was taken to Lahore, and the square where it happened is part of Shahidganj.
